A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with the same authors, relative-improvement framework, and principal theoretical results. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 provides analytic population-risk illustrations, including Figures 1 and 4, but reports no experimental, sampled-simulation, or observed-data study. Section 5 develops an empirical estimator theoretically without reporting experimental outcomes.

after.justification: Section 6 and Appendix G report original analyses of 2018 ACS income data across 50 states, including 400 partition–feature configurations and comparisons among fairness methods.

M1.justification: The relative-improvement objective, empirical estimator, and leximin refinement remain unchanged. Appendix G documents numerical implementations for the added experiments, without establishing a revision to the proposed method.

E1.justification: v2 adds ACS log-income prediction for full-time, year-round employees across all 50 states, partitioned by sex and race. This introduces substantial real-data population and task coverage beyond v1's analytic examples; the theoretical regression, classification, and RKHS settings remain.

E2.justification: Figures 5, 8, and 10 introduce an empirical comparison of MMRI against ERM, Group DRO, MMV, MMR, and Nash. v1 compared MMR in its analytic example and other criteria schematically or axiomatically; ERM and Nash newly participate in reported performance comparisons.

E3.justification: The added ACS evaluation fits linear models with intercepts, group-specific oracles, and a constant-mean baseline, sweeping 10,001 group weights to construct frontiers. It evaluates single-feature and four-feature models using per-group RMSE, relative improvement, and oracle-gap ratios. These are new experimental protocols, not demonstrated reruns of an existing evaluation.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds six case studies examining how unequal predictability affects method allocations. Its single-feature versus four-feature comparison tests whether gap asymmetry persists with richer inputs. These provide empirical sensitivity and failure-mode analyses beyond v1's constructed illustrations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Table 2's new across-state ranges, medians, and proportions describe heterogeneity rather than uncertainty in performance estimates.

E6.justification: Figure 1 replaces the analytic MMR outcomes (−56%, 87%) and RI outcomes (69%, 69%) with ACS North Dakota outcomes of (−74%, 82%) and (57%, 57%), respectively; these are different settings, not performance changes under a common setting. Section 6 and Appendix G add extensive results, including gap ratios from 0.04 to 3.48 and only 27% near-symmetric configurations.

T1.justification: The central axiom characterization changes substantively: Proposition 4.2 restricts individual monotonicity to expansions preserving other groups' optimal risks and replaces exchangeability-based symmetry with permutation equivariance. Proposition 4.4 and Table 1 are adjusted accordingly, including correcting egalitarian methods' IM entries. Theorem 5.4 tightens its condition from Δ/2 to Δ/4, matching the corrected 2ε0 denominator bound. Appendix D also removes unsupported strict-convexity and growth-bound assertions.

C1.justification: The abstract and discussion retain the principal contributions: fairness as bargaining, relative improvement as the KS solution, axiomatic justification, no-harm guarantees, and finite-sample convergence. The new introduction contribution list organizes these existing claims, while the ACS evidence supports the retained heterogeneous-predictability motivation.

C2.justification: New Appendix C substantially explains baseline dependence, interpretable defaults, and why pooled ERM or an existing Pareto compromise is generally unsuitable as the disagreement baseline. Remark 4.5 explicitly recommends choosing criteria by contextual axioms rather than universal preference for RI. Appendix G adds interpretations of demographic predictability differences and their persistence with additional features.

D1.justification: Appendix G supplies new reproducibility information: ACS access through folktables, employment filters, target transformation, feature encodings, weighted least-squares fitting, baseline and oracle construction, and frontier resolution. It also describes ERM warm-start and exponentiated group-weight updates, although numerical optimization hyperparameters and a held-out evaluation split are not specified.

R1.justification: v2 adds Zafar et al. (2017), distinguishing earlier bargaining-inspired preference fairness from its explicit bargaining formulation. It also adds Ding et al. (2021) and Korenman and Neumark (1991) for the empirical material and removes the CFPB credit-invisibility reference. The broader related-work structure remains.

P1.justification: v2 adds an explicit contribution list, inserts an experimental section, expands baseline and figure explanations, and makes localized wording corrections. Existing sections and appendices largely retain their wording and ordering, with renumbering accommodating the additions.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn around the ACS example, and v2 adds Figure 5, Table 2, and the multi-panel empirical Figures 8–10. These substantially expand the visual presentation. Existing conceptual figures are retained, including v1 Figures 5–6 as v2 Figures 6–7.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central motivation with ACS evidence that unequal group predictability and problematic absolute-scale allocations occur in real data, extending v1's analytic illustrations. It also corrects an overstated monotonicity condition and a convergence-bound error, while explaining the consequential baseline choice. The experiments lack reported held-out validation and uncertainty estimates, but the gains in empirical grounding and theoretical precision are substantial.
